what: Sotera Health sterilises medical devices and tests drugs and devices for safety. Its Sterigenics unit sterilises a large share of the world’s single-use medical products with ethylene oxide gas and gamma radiation; Nordion supplies the cobalt-60 used for gamma sterilisation; and Nelson Labs tests products for medical device and pharmaceutical makers.
customers: Medical device makers such as Medtronic, Becton Dickinson and Johnson & Johnson, and pharmaceutical companies.
money: Contract sterilisation of syringes, gowns, catheters and implants.
Supply of the radioactive isotope used in gamma sterilisation.
Lab testing of medical devices and drugs.
moat: Sterilisation capacity is regulated, slow to build and essential: hospitals cannot use most medical products without it. Sotera and Steris together dominate the outsourced market, and Nordion is one of only a few suppliers of cobalt-60.
risks: Lawsuits over ethylene oxide emissions near its plants have cost hundreds of millions in settlements, and more claims are pending.
Environmental rules on ethylene oxide are tightening, which raises costs.
It is controlled by private equity firms that have sold shares over time.
opportunities: Revenue has grown every year, from $931M in 2021 to $1.23B over the last twelve months.
Its services are essential and recurring: medical device makers cannot skip sterilisation.
Free cash flow is recovering as large capital projects finish.
Nine analysts average a $21 target, about 33% above the price.
watch: Legal settlements and capital spending on emission controls.
view: Sotera runs an essential, high-margin service in a near-duopoly, yet its shares trade at a discount because of the lawsuits. Communities near its ethylene oxide plants have sued over emissions, and settlements have cost hundreds of millions of dollars, which is why 2022 showed a large loss and 2023 negative cash flow.
Strip that out and the business is steady: revenue up every year, recurring demand from medical device makers and pricing power. The forward P/E of about 16 assumes the legal costs keep falling.

This turns on litigation. If remaining claims settle at manageable cost, the shares look cheap for a business of this quality. I would call it a reasonable bet with a legal discount attached, and the debt means it cannot absorb many more large settlements.
bull: Legal claims settle, cash flow recovers and the market re-rates an essential service business.
bear: New lawsuits or tighter emissions rules keep costs high and debt limits flexibility.
